opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting directions we can take, and honestly, I think it's almost inevitable if we take continual learning seriously. When we talk about a system that learns from its own stream of experience over a long period of time, we usually focus on the weights. The structure is fixed, and learning means adjusting the parameters inside that structure. But if you look at biological systems, and at the kinds of tasks we care about in my lab, like prosthetic limbs that people wear and use every day for years, that fixed-structure assumption starts to look quite limiting.

A person's needs change. Their body changes, their environment changes, the tasks they want to do change. A system that has to partner with that person over the long haul can't know ahead of time what representation it's going to need. So the question becomes: can the agent use its own experience to decide where it needs more capacity, which features are useful, which aren't pulling their weight, and how to reorganize itself?

There's been some lovely work in this area. Rich Sutton and others have talked for a long time about generate-and-test approaches: the system proposes new features, keeps the ones that prove useful, and discards or recycles the ones that don't. More recently there's been attention on loss of plasticity in deep networks, the observation that standard networks trained continually get worse at learning over time. One remedy is to keep refreshing parts of the network, reinitializing units that aren't contributing. That's already a small step toward a system modifying its own structure based on what it has experienced.

From my perspective, the really interesting part is that it ties structure to prediction. In our work, much of what an agent knows is expressed as predictions about its future sensations and signals, things like general value functions. If an agent can tell which predictions are hard to make, or where its errors are persistently high, that's a signal about where it needs new representational resources. The architecture then grows out of the agent's interaction with the world rather than being handed down by a designer.

There are challenges, of course. You have to manage computational budgets, avoid catastrophic changes, and keep the system stable enough that the person relying on it can trust it. In assistive technology, you can't have a prosthetic arm suddenly reorganize itself in a way that surprises the user. So there's a real design question about how fast and how visibly that adaptation happens, and how the human stays part of the loop.

But philosophically, I'd say yes, absolutely. If we want machines that are genuinely adaptive partners, they have to be able to change not just what they know but how they're built to know it. Experience should shape the mind, not just fill it in.

r001.rationale: The response presents architecture adaptation from experience as an active area of work and raises unresolved questions about how to allocate capacity, preserve stability, and involve the human user.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think this is actually one of the most exciting and, honestly, one of the most underexplored frontiers in the field right now. For a long time we've treated the architecture of a learning system as something fixed by the designer. You pick the number of layers, the width, the connectivity, you train it, and then you deploy it. The learning that happens is all about adjusting the weights inside a structure that someone else decided on ahead of time.

But if you take continual learning seriously, meaning an agent that's embedded in a stream of experience that never stops, that has to keep adapting for its entire operational lifetime, then that picture starts to look pretty limiting. The world the agent is in is going to change. The tasks it faces are going to change. And it seems very strange to say that the one thing allowed to stay frozen is the shape of the computational substrate itself.

So the idea of a system using its own experience to decide where it needs more capacity, where it can prune away structure it's no longer using, how it should wire new features into the things it's already learned, I find that very natural. It's closer to how biological systems work. Brains grow new connections, they lose connections, they reorganize based on what they're actually doing in the world. And one of the things that's really shaped my thinking here is the work that's come out of Rich Sutton's group and others on things like generate-and-test approaches, where you're constantly proposing new features, keeping the ones that turn out to be useful for prediction, and discarding the ones that aren't. That's a form of experience-driven architecture change, even if it's a fairly simple one.

Now, I'd put a couple of caveats on it. One is that this has to be driven by signals the agent actually has access to from its own stream, things like prediction error, or how much a given unit is contributing to the agent's ability to predict and control its sensorimotor data. It can't rely on an outside designer stepping in. And the second is that it needs to be computationally cheap enough to happen online, in real time, as the agent is acting. If restructuring the network requires stopping everything and retraining from scratch, that's not really continual learning anymore.

So in short, I view it as a necessary direction rather than an optional one. If we want agents that are true lifelong learners, operating alongside people over months and years, then letting experience shape not just what the network knows but what the network is, seems to me to be a core part of the picture.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls experience-driven architecture change “one of the most underexplored frontiers” in the field, clearly presenting it as an open research problem.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really interesting possibility. We often think about learning as changing the weights within a fixed network, but there’s no fundamental reason that the structure itself has to remain fixed. A system’s experience could help determine what representations it needs, where it needs more capacity, and what it can let go of.

The challenge is deciding when those changes are useful. If you’re continually learning, changing your architecture also changes the substrate that holds what you’ve already learned. So you need to be able to adapt without constantly disrupting abilities that are still valuable.

For me, the key question is how that process is grounded in interaction. Does a structural change help the system make better predictions, act more effectively, or learn something new more efficiently? That’s what would make it compelling: architecture becoming another part of how the system adapts through experience.

r001.rationale: The response presents experience-driven architecture changes as a possibility and identifies unresolved challenges and a key research question about when such changes help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very natural part of continual learning. If a system is going to learn over a lifetime, we shouldn’t necessarily expect the structure we give it on day one to be the right structure for everything it encounters. Its experience could help determine not just the values of its parameters, but what representations it needs and how much capacity to devote to them.

The interesting question is what drives those changes. Can the system recognize that its current representation is inadequate, add something useful, and then assess whether that addition actually improves its predictions or its ability to act? And can it do that while preserving the knowledge it already depends on?

So I see changing architecture as part of the broader problem of adapting your learning resources through experience. You want a system that can grow when growth is useful, reuse what it has learned, and keep learning without having to start over.

r001.rationale: It frames architecture changes driven by experience as an unresolved question, asking how a system can detect inadequate representations, add capacity, and assess the result while preserving existing knowledge.
